The country has the use of the plant during the war.

And we pay for it. I refer now to P.C. 7819, made with the Falconbridge Nickel Mines Limited. Under the same act, this company was assured of a contract through the war production board of the United States to purchase ten million pounds of nickel in matte during 1942 to 1945 at a price which included six cents a pound extra to repay the company, over the life of the contract, for the capital costs incurred in fulfilling the order. The company claimed that unless special depreciation allowances were granted to enable the company to amortize the costs of the additional facilities in mine, mill and smelter over the life of the three-year contract, the expenditure necessary to provide the facilities would be wholly unjustified on account of the small net return and doubtful value of the additional plant and facilities after the war. Now what does the government allow? The government has allowed the company, in computing the amount of profits for purposes of the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, a deduction by way of special depreciation allowance as follows: for the year 1942, twenty per cent of the cost of depreciable assets, not to exceed $131,346; and for each of the years 1943 and 1944-each of the years-forty per cent of the cost of the depreciable assets, not to exceed $262,690 in each of the three years. And who is going to own the plant and the depreciated assets at the end of the three years? This nickel company.
What is wrong with that?

The other day I asked some questions in the house about the Ship-shaw development. I wish to say that I object to the government of Canada giving anything to either the nickel company or the aluminum company. The Aluminum Company of Canada Limited was the predominant partner in the Alliance Aluminum Company of Basle, Switzerland, in 1931, when the world was divided up among German and other companies. I do not want to name them all.
Why not?

Because, to be perfectly frank about it, I do not happen to have them on the tip of my tongue. The Aluminum
The Budfjet-Mr. Coldwell

Company of Canada was the predominant partner when the markets were allotted in July, 1931; it had the largest amounts allotted to it of any company. What do we find? We find that that agreement stated in effect-and they varied that agreement a little later on so that they would not interfere with one another in the export market-that each member of the Alliance could manufacture up to the limit in its own domestic market. We find to-day, as a result of that policy, that we have to gather up the old aluminum pots and pans throughout this country and in the United States because during these years, under that agreement, the Germans had built up the largest aluminum development in the whole world.
Oh, no, the United States has the largest.

I can give my hon. friend the figures. I am not speaking without having studied this matter fairly intensively during the past few weeks and examined the records of the committee which sat in the United States the other day.
If you look at International Nickel and the other nickel companies you find the same thing. Yet under policies like this we are handing oyer the control of plants and resources to these powerful monopolistic industries which will, if they have the opportunity, regain some sort of liaison with the great companies in the countries with which we are at war Therefore I say that I object strenuously to the alienation of our resources and the depreciation of our national investments in this manner to companies of this description.
One other example-
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but he has exceeded his time.
I moved a subamendment, Mr. Speaker.

As the hon. member says, he moved a subamendment. But I have examined the question whether the hon. member is entitled to longer than forty minutes, and I have come to the conclusion that he cannot be permitted to continue beyond that time except with the unanimous consent of the house.
Go on.

Thank you. May I point this out, that last year, when the hon. member for Lethbridge was in exactly the same position as I am in to-night, he was allowed to continue, and it was stated that he had the right to continue. I did not think of bringing down this evening the copy of

Hansard which bears on that point because I did not think the matter would be raised. Had I done so, I would have been quite prepared to discuss the question.
Go ahead.
Let us have a ruling.

I have no recollection that such a privilege was given to the hon. member for Lethbridge; but I was considering, while the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr, Coldwell) was speaking, whether the point might arise, and I think the house is entitled to know the reason why I should object to the hon, member continuing.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if there is any question about it-
Let us hear Mr. Speaker's ruling.

If the hon. member with the consent of the house wishes to continue longer, of course the Chair will agree; but in the circumstances here perhaps it might be well if a ruling came from the Chair, because the same situation arose on the debate on the address; the question was then raised, but not presented to the Chair for any decision. I think it might be well that the hon. member should continue, because that appears to be the feeling of the house. Nevertheless, for the guidance of hon. members in future, I think the house should know the position I would take with regard to this question.
Let us have the ruling.

Standing order 37 states:
No member, except the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, or a minister moving a government order and the member speaking in reply immediately after such minister, or a member making a motion of "no confidence" in the government and a minister replying thereto, shall speak for more than forty minutes at a time in any debate.
A close examination of that standing order shows that it had been drafted without having in view the complex situation which has arisen, as we have it to-night, and as we had it during the previous debate on the address. The principle that each amendment or subamendment is a separate question only applies to relevancy and to the right of a member to speak again. It has no relation to the special rule limiting the length of speeches, and it does not alter the fact that when the house is seized of a motion of want of confidence all the allegations which make up that motion must be decided together. Members may vote against the amendment and for the motion, or

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
vice versa. In any event the final decision of the house can be ascertained only after the amendment has passed through all its proposed alterations, and resolved on its final phraseology which will be the real motion of *want of confidence put by the Chair. Such a motion cannot be divided.
The hon. member's subamendment is as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets the failure of the government to provide for the nationalization of the banking system so as to make possible the full utilization of the Bank of Canada for the financing of the war;
And further this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for increases in the amounts paid to old age and blind pensioners, or to make adequate provisions for veterans of the last or the present war, or their widows and dependents;
And further this house regrets the extent to which the government has vested the control of the Canadian economy in monopolistic industry and finance."
That is an amplification of the motion of want of confidence, as embodied in the amendment of the hon. member for Lethbridge. There cannot be two motions of want of confidence at the same time before the house. There is only one now, and it consists of the amendment together with the subamendment. The vote on the subamendment will not be final, but it will have to be followed by the question: " Shall the amendment as amended carry?" If it carries, "no confidence" will have been voted against the government. For these reasons I rule that the hon. member is not entitled to speak longer than forty minutes.
However, if there is unanimous consent of the house, 1 presume the hon. member may continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Mr. Speaker, in view of your last statement, although perhaps not strictly in order I should like to mention the reason why I think all hon. members ought to permit the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) to continue his speech at least to a reasonable degree. My reason is this: Under a friendly arrangement, on a major debate it has been arranged that one of them shall precede the other, and that in a following debate the other should come first. As hon. members know, this arrangement gives the leader who speaks first the right to move an amendment to the main motion, thereby gaining the right to address the house without restriction.
Order.
Under those circumstances I appeal to hon. members to permit the hon. member to proceed.
Where are you going to draw the line?

I have given my ruling.
The hon. member for Parry Sound must realize that when a question is put to the Chair all the Chair can do is to give an interpretation of the rule. I have endeavoured to do so, and in my judgment the hon. member cannot continue, under the rules. However, with unanimous consent the house may permit the hon. member to proceed, and I take it that it is the wish of hon. members that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar should have that privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Go ahead.
I shall draw my remarks as rapidly as possible to a close-
Go ahead.
-leaving out some of the things I had intended to say.
Go on; the Liberals want to hear you.

Well, I am glad to
know the Liberals are courteous enough to want to hear me; but I believe the hon. member who has just interrupted will agree with me when I say I have not spared the Liberal government to-night.
I am always interested.

Before taking my seat I wish to say something about some other matters which are related to the ones I have just mentioned, and which I believe are disturbing. I am not going into this fully tonight, because there will be other opportunities. I am, however, thinking of the tremendous expansion which has occurred in the last four years in the air transport system of Canada. I am thinking, too, of the fact that when we set up the Trans-Canada Air Lines it was generally understood that years ago we had made a mistake in not keeping the railways as a national organization. It was pointed out that at least we ought to keep the air free for the people, and unalienated in any degree. And yet during the past year we have witnessed the tremendous growth of the new Canadian Pacific air lines. We notice a statement from L. B. Unwin, president of the Canadian Pacific lines, in -which he states:
During its first year of operations Canadian Pacific Airlines flew approximately 6,000,000 schedule airplane miles in 1942.
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

Passengers and mail carried were more than double the previous year. Air cargo reached a record total of close to 10,000,000 pounds. The company now employes over 6,000 employees in its commercial operations, air training schools and overhaul plants.
Then we are told that it played a major role in the construction of the Alaska highway. It did.

It shows
what a private enterprise will do.

A private enterprise
based on heavy expenditures made by the people of Canada. What have we done? We have provided them with all the facilities required. We have provided the long and more expensive hauls across the country, leaving the short and more profitable hauls in the hands of the private organization. Let us remember that it entered the field only since the war. And what it has built up to date has been built through war traffic, mainly through carrying government men, government equipment and government freight.
What about it in the post-war period? Well, we have to watch. The president the other day was quite frank in this statement:
In this regard the Canadian Pacific, as a long established world-wide transport system, will undoubtedly through the extension of its air operations, take its natural place in the development of world trade and travel routes.
In past months I have had some little opportunity to sit in on discussions dealing with post-war air traffic, and I want to say that as a country we are making a mistake if we do not do what other countries are doing, namely, safeguard our airways, and our own publicly owned air corporation.
In the United States they have the great Pan-American Airways Limited, a private organization. I say that that organization, in seeking to gain control of certain airways in this world, will create considerable difficulties for the great nation to the south of us, and make it more difficult, in some respects, perhaps, even to reach the kind of international agreements we want to reach.
It is backed by the United States government.

Great Britain has kept her airways under her control, Imperial airways, British airways, government controlled organizations, and we should see to it that since we control the vital air route between great populated areas of the world in Europe and Asia we do not allow the alienation of our great air routes.
There are one or two other observations I wish to make, but I will be very brief. We
[Mr. Coldwell.)
are pleased that the government has adopted the pay-as-you-go plan of income tax payment. We are under no illusions, however; we know we are going to pay more this year in most of the brackets. But I believe the change will -relieve a good many people of worry about the hang-over from the previous year, and with the high taxes we have I think it is important that we should have no hang-over of any description, if I may put it in that way. I am pleased also that the minister has exempted government annuities; that is something that I thought it was a pity was not done last year.
He has not told us that.
Oh, yes, that is the intimation in the budget speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether hon.. gentlemen are thinking about the same thing.
I stated in the budget speech that payments on government annuities purchased before the date of last year's budget and being paid before that date would be allowed as offsets against the refundable tax.

That is right, placing such annuities on the same basis as life insurance was on the same date. I am very sorry that we are continuing the system of encouraging prospecting by mining companies by means of rebates of their war taxes. I think again we are allowing the alienation of our natural resources to private corporations when the time has come when we ought to be doing some of this prospecting and developing; ourselves.
In relation to income taxes generally, I suggest to the minister that while the computation of farmers' income taxes on a two-year basis is better than on a one-year basis, speaking particularly for the farmers in the prairie provinces where we sometimes have quite long: periods of drought and disaster, that period is not long enough. It should be an average of five years, or three years at the very least.
We from the prairies are disturbed about the threat that we hear that the cooperative societies may be assessed for income tax. We hear rumours to that effect. I suggest to the minister that he follow the example of other countries where cooperatives have been in existence for a long time and treat them here as they are treated there. These societies are not corporations; they are simply mutual aid societies, not out for profit making but purely to perform a service, and anything that accrues to the members in the way of patronage dividends is incidental to the real purpose of the society.

The Budget-Mr. Turgeon
I did intend to say something about the national debt, but I shall leave that until the resolutions are under discussion. I want to thank the house for the courtesy it has extended to me to-night. I did not wish to trespass upon the time of the house beyond my forty minutes when I discovered that was all I was entitled to, and I am very grateful for having been given this courtesy.

I know that the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth party (Mr. Coldwell) who has just taken his seat will excuse me if for a moment only I deal with some of the incidents of the last twenty or twenty-five minutes. First may I say, partly in joke but only partly so, that I [DOT]could see a little chuckle of delight on the part of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) at the commencement of the hon. member's address when he took issue with the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) over the allegation that the province of Saskatchewan is in worse shape than the province of Alberta. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture was delighted to hear a defence of the government of Saskatchewan.
Anything but that.

I know, but that was the effect. The other thought I want to express in connection with his general statements is as to what he said about this government permitting private air companies to operate. What will be the proper solution of our air problem when this war is over is a question on which at the moment I cannot state an opinion. It may be the duty of Canadians to see that Trans-Canada Air Lines is enlarged so as to include all air transport. Personally I am doubtful of it. But what I wish to point out is that if what the hon. member said to-night had been the considered policy of this government during the last ten years, all that part of British Columbia known as the Cariboo country, which extends almost from within touch of Vancouver city clear to the Yukon and across the mountains to the Northwest Territories would have been without its one saving feature in transportation; it would have been without airways. The first air company operating in that whole part of British Columbia was the originator of the Yukon Southern. It was greatly extended until that part of British Columbia north of the main line of the Canadian National Railways from Edmonton to Prince Rupert had an air service where before it had no transportation whatever except seasonally down the waterways. That air service was then extended until Vancouver and the Peace
River block, White Horse in the Yukon Territory and Edmonton were all connected by air service. And it was only after those air services were in operation and that part of British Columbia enabled to come in small measure into its own that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company came in and bought out the existing companies. If it is the considered policy of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken to see that no private companies be permitted to run in such areas as that, I must take exception to it.
Before speaking on the budget and in connection with money matters, with which parliament naturally has so much to do, I wish to say a word concerning my young and very good friend the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and to congratulate him and the Progressive Conservative party upon its choice of him as its leader in this house. The hon. member has been in my constituency; he has been in that part of the Cariboo which started the population trend in British Columbia, that part where the Cariboo gold rush took place. He has not been in the other part of my constituency which is becoming famous on account of the very air services of which I was speaking a few moments ago. Speaking here to-night, I want to tell all the supporters of the Progressive Conservative party in my constituency that they can be satisfied that they have conducting their party affairs in this house an honest, good Canadian.
But may I express just a word or two of wonderment. Since he has taken over the leadership of his party in this house I have noticed that, quite naturally, he has been very proud of the word "Progressive" which has been attached to the word "Conservative" in the re-naming of the party. I am inclined to think that the Winnipeg conference was an excellent thing for the Conservative party, and I believe it will turn out to be a good thing for Canada, because it has helped to focus. attention upon the need for reform. It has directed attention to those groups of men and women who in days gone by, when reform was not as popular as it is to-day, were trying to bring about a condition under which reform could take root and grow.
* Since the Winnipeg convention, every time the government has made any suggestion of a movement looking to reform, either the leader of the Progressive Conservative party or someone behind him has stated that the inspiration came from the Winnipeg convention. He has not yet claimed that the Atlantic charter was inspired by that convention; and while at that convention many
The Budget-Mr. Turgeon

glowing references were made to our relations with the United States, neither has he claimed that the Ogdensburg agreement or the Hyde Park agreement, which followed from it, were inspired by the Winnipeg convention. However, as I have said, it is a good thing that the Winnipeg convention took place. The Progressive Conservative party have confessed and have repented, though I am afraid they will have to remain in sackcloth and ashes for quite a while yet. I feel certain that if the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) were sitting in the place of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), he would say to my friends opposite, as St. Matthew said, "Are you simply fleeing from the wrath to come?"
I should now like to put on record a letter that I received some years ago. There is no doubt at all that throughout Canada there is suspicion of men in public life. That has not come about only during the last few years. I can remember when I was first elected to a seat in the legislative assembly of Alberta, away back in 1913. I had not been a member of that legislature very long until I could feel that I was not held in quite such high regard as I had been before I permitted myself to become a candidate on behalf of a political party, and had the good or bad luck to be elected. We in this house have been talking a good deal about reconstruction, and a great deal has been said about what members of parliament and what parliament itself should do. Hon. members must not permit themselves to forget the suspicion with which I am dealing, which is felt by many people in Canada with regard to men who are in public life. To-day the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party read a resolution which was proposed by the present Prime Minister at the Liberal convention which took place in 1919. I should like to read a letter in order to show how the Prime Minister has been viewing these matters of reform ever since 1919. This letter comes from the office of the leader of the opposition in Ottawa and is dated April 2, 1931:
J. G-. Turgeon, Esquire,
744 Hastings Street West,
Vancouver, B.C.
My dear Turgeon:
I thank you for sending me a copy of your recent interesting address before the Progressive Liberal Association.
With your general point of view I am, as you would know, in complete accord. I question, however, the wisdom of including in the Liberal programme the policy of state life

insurance until, at least, we have succeeded in getting a national system of social insurance, which will include unemployment, accident, invalidity, old age, etcetera. The worst feature of the social insurance problem to-day is that each province is attempting to cope with it more or less in its own fashion. What is needed is a national scheme which will provide like standards in all the provinces. I am inclined to think that there should be a readjustment of the financial relations between the dominion and the provinces, which would involve, on the one hand, either a lessening or eliminating of federal subsidies, and on the other, the assumption by the federal government of social insurance obligations in the directions indicated. It is a large reform and I recognize it is full of difficulties, arising out of the desire of the provinces to continue their control in many of these matters. Sooner or later, however, the change will be made and I, for one, would be happy if it should come in our lifetime. Personally, I feel that the time to take on a programme of state life insurance, if it is to be taken on, would be after headway had been made in the other direction.
With kind regards,
Yours sincerely,
.	W. L. Mackenzie King.
That letter was written to me after I had sent the Prime Minister a newspaper report of a speech I had made before a Liberal association-a Progressive Liberal association- in Vancouver, in which I urged that the Liberal party should give consideration to the insurance problems affecting the people of Canada, with a view to seeing, first, whether the Liberal party should recommend a programme of state life insurance or, second, whether the Liberal party should recommend that there be a cooperative effort between the great insurance companies and the governments of Canada, so that the experience and knowledge of the insurance companies should not be lost but that at the same time we should not lose sight of the human values and the human welfare which could be put into insurance in greater measure by governmental motivation and under governmental direction.
I listened to some of the speeches made during the last debate, and I have read newspaper accounts of speeches made in this house and outside about the inspiration that came to the Prime Minister from Winnipeg. I thought immediately of that particular letter, and I know that every member in this house perhaps can think of conversations he has had relating to matters of reform which would on their own prove that one of the great motivating desires of the Prime Minister throughout the years has been gradually to bring about a condition where human welfare and human needs will be the foundation of a higher and better standard of life.
The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) covered a great deal of ground1 when speak-

The Budget-Mr. Turgeon
ing last night and to-day. Among other things he referred to the way in which the House of Commons sitting either as a house or in committees, deals with public affairs in connection with governmental expenditures. He threw out a warning to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and through him to the government. He warned that the things that are being done are not being properly publicized, and he referred particularly to labour. He said that labour was told about the lack of fuel and about the hardships which a condition of war imposed upon the people of Canada, but he said that labour was not told properly of the great things that were being done, such as keeping down inflation.
As I listened to the hon. member, I thought of the attempt which is being made to show the people of Canada a certain side of affairs which might possibly have some foundation. Reference was made yesterday to graft in connection with the carrying out of some contract. If the hon. member for Danforth is right and we are making a mistake and not properly building up the morale of the people of Canada by telling them of the good things being done by this government, are not those-I speak now without the slightest thought of criticism, I am thinking only of war morale- who are referring to the hiding of certain things which they claim are taking place, making an effort, without knowing it, to destroy public morale?
I remember, and I think every other hon. member will remember-again I am speaking without any critical attitude-the days before the war when the time of this House of Commons and the people of Canada was taken up for a year or a year and a half by an investigation into the Bren gun contract. Again remember that I am not talking critically because that event is past. But if Hitler himself, in the preparations for war against the world which he then was making, had asked any body of Canadians to help him, what more could have been done for him than to stop the government of Canada for a year and a half immediately prior to the war from making the efforts then made under the direction of the minister from British Columbia to prepare for war days.

Examining
a contract does not stop you from making machine guns.
To examine the contract in the manner in which my hon. friend and some others were speaking yesterday, would give the same result as the examining of the Bren gun contract.
It did.

It did break up the
morale of the people and stopped us from taking our proper place in the first year of the war.
It got you a much better contract.
You wanted it rescinded; you did everything possible to stop it.
They wanted it cancelled.

I am speaking without any thought of criticism and in all seriousness. We are facing what will be the most tragic days we have ever had. It will not be long before our boys overseas will be engaged in a slaughter, perhaps unequalled since the war began. I am asking members of this house to be careful of the way in which public opinion is aroused in these days of preparation for what is coming to us from overseas.
Speaking of the way in which the House of Commons conducts its business, I intend to take the liberty of putting on the record something which is rather old. This is taken from the official records of the legislative assembly of Alberta. It is a motion presented by me on March 2, 1920, just 23 years ago, and it reads:
Moved by Mr. Turgeon, seconded by Mr. Davidson:
Whereas under the generally accepted interpretation of the working of the British parliamentary system it is assumed that the defeat of a bill or measure presented to the legislative assembly by a minister of the crown officially on behalf of the government is in itself a defeat of the government; and
Whereas the members of this legislative assembly feel that the time has come when members ought to be free to vote either for or against any bill or measure before the house without thereby expressing lack of confidence in the government;
Therefore be it resolved that this house express its desire that the premier ought not to consider the defeat of any government measure a sufficient reason for tendering the resignation of his government, unless such defeat be followed by a vote of non-confidenee in the government.
In 1923, about three years after, an hon. member from Alberta who then sat in this house introduced a similar motion, but it was not carried either. I proposed that motion not because I was young and did not know what it was all about, but because conditions were such that it seemed to me as a member of the assembly that a resolution of that kind was essential if we were to have parliamentary government. I have been in Ottawa for seven years since 1935, and I take the liberty of saying that I now firmly believe that the
The Budget-Mr. Turgeon

motion which I have just read and which I presented many years ago is not needed in this House of Commons in Ottawa.
Why is it not needed? I should like to answer those who are critical of the manner in which the business of parliament is carried on. I have heard it said here, and I have read it in the newspapers that members on the government side of the house were merely rubber stamps. I think that was said yesterday. We have been told also that when committees are set up, the government members on those committees are instructed as to what attitude they must take and they follow those instructions. I am not a rubber stamp. I have been a faithful member of this government and of the Liberal party, but I am not a rubber stamp.
I have been on some important committees of this house. I was on the defence of Canada regulations committee under the chairmanship of the Minister of Finance, and I was on the pensions committee of last session. This session I am on the reconstruction committee. On no occasion has any minister of the crown ever made the slightest suggestion to me as to what should be my attitude toward any question coming up before any of these committees. During last session I happened to be chairman of one of the committees. At no time has any suggestion ever been made to me about the attitude I should adopt on that committee in connection with any question whatsoever.
I attend faithfully the caucuses of the Liberal party. A great deal has been said about government caucuses and1 about the whip hand held over members on the government side of the house. I can speak of the whips because I have been the deputy chief government whip, and the whips, in Canada at least, are simply the organizers of the business of parliament. They work hard and well without any remuneration, and I should like to take this opportunity of paying tribute to all those men who during this parliament and the last have been whips for the different parties. I cannot speak of caucuses of the Progressive Conservative party, or of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, or of the Social Credit party, or of any of the newly-formed independent parties in the house, but I can speak for the Liberal party and say that every member of the Liberal party emerges from a Liberal caucus just as free as when he entered.
And just as pure.

Somebody says, "and just as pure." I say that he leaves the caucus just as free as when he entered it. There is nothing binding on any member on this side of the house through his attending the caucuses of the party. For these reasons I say that this motion which I have made, in spite of the fact that I was a supporter of the government in powrer as I still am, was not in the least degree needed in this House of Commons.
Just one further word with respect to the speech of the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, and I mention it in closing because I want to throw out in that connection a suggestion or two about my own constituency. The hon. member spoke of prospectors and denounced the arrangement made by the Minister of Finance for prospectors to go out into the country where minerals abound and prospect for them. I must say that if the hon. member's advice were taken, semi-ruination would come to certain parts of the constituency of Cariboo and to other constituencies in British Columbia.

He did not
speak of prospecting by individuals, but by mining companies, giving them concessions.

He used the term
"prospectors" and said that all that work should be done by the government. If my hon. friend will look at Hansard to-morrow he will see that the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) used the term "prospectors".	.
He was speaking of prospecting by mining companies, not by individual prospectors.

That is prospecting. What I was about to say when my hon, friend interrupted, which interruption I do not resent in the least, is that some years ago as a result of the discovery of fraudulent practices by some of the brokerage companies the provinces became panic-stricken and passed certain legislation which almost killed prospecting, and to-day British Columbia is full of old prospectors who, because they could obtain nothing for their discoveries, found it useless to go on their prospecting trips. Therefore, while my hon. friends opposite may be sad, I was happy when the Minister of Finance arranged for a reduction of taxation to permit prospecting again to take place.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I express the hope that the Minister of Finance will always keep one thing positively in his mind when dealing with the financial administration of this country. I feel for the farmers; I

The Budget-Mr. Lacombe
feel for labour; I feel for industry; I feel for the aged people; I feel for the workers in industry. But the one thing which this government must never forget is that no matter where the money is to come from, when our men come back from overseas, from the air force, the army, the navy and the merchant marine, when this war is over, there must be no question of giving them relief, but instead they must be assured of a proper standard of living based upon emploj'ment, and for those who are disabled a proper standard of living based upon a disability pension. In this connection I recommend to the government, to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) and the ministers of the defence departments, that they give further consideration to the proposal to restore the insurance principle in pensions. With that thought, Mr. Speaker, and . with one word more of praise and appreciation of the efforts of the Minister of Pensions and National Health, I conclude.

Mr. Speaker, the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) caused quite a commotion among many people of this country and it will cause many more to be startled. Is it fair to bear down in such a manner as this budget does upon the taxpayer who is in receipt of a small income? What are the intentions of the government? On the one hand it passes measures of social security, and then on the other hand it counteracts the effects of those measures by levying taxes so heavy that they threaten both the family and society. It is certainly not in the best interests of the country to spend sums so enormous that the whole economy of the nation is threatened and in danger of crumbling under the weight of taxation. If the Canadian people are compelled to accept the sacrifices called for in this budget, certainly they will not be capable of bearing them all. We are already bending down under the weight of the present excessive taxation, and now the government imposes still more and'more taxation. Our man-power, our economic and financial position will not be able to absorb these billions of new taxation. The government is leading the country to bankruptcy without a thought for agriculture and the working classes who are the main source of the substance and man-power required for the production of food and munitions.
What is the government doing to remedy the lack of man-power in the agricultural domain which is threatening our production of food? On March 1, the hon. member for 72537-71
Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) denounced in this house the capitalists who are taking advantage of the present state of war in order to exploit small owners. Their greed is becoming even greater. During many years the farmers and the consumers have been the victims of the trusts of this country. The proof is found in the high prices paid for fertilizers and feedstuffs which are necessary to agricultural production. The rationing of butter and sugar deprives the consumer of the first necessities of life, while there are millions of pounds of butter stored away in warehouses. The farmer will not be able fully to develop his sugar bush and thus provide against the rationing of tea and sugar. There is in Canada an ever-increasing scarcity of beef, veal and pork. Why this ridiculous situation in a country overflowing with wheat and the grain by-products which form the basis of dairy feedstuffs? The government should at least prevent the large milling combinations and all greedy intermediaries from exploiting farmers and consumers. Who will dare contradict me on this point, *when everyone knows that wheat sells for the ridiculous price of eighty cents or ninety cents a bushel, while the consumer must pay almost four dollars for 100 pounds of wheat flour? Who will claim that I am distorting facts, when feedstuffs, by-products of wheat flour, sell as high as 12.75 and $2.90 per 100 pounds? If you add to all this the military call-up of farmers and war workers, you will have the real causes of the agricultural, industrial and economic turmoil which is afflicting this country. What measure is this budget proposing to remedy this deplorable state of affairs? It is imposing new taxes which affect the small owners and the working classes. This is where our participation in this war is leading us- unrestricted participation, and consequently a participation above our strength.
On September 9, 1939, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, I condemned this participation. This is where it is leading us, this mobilization act which was adopted on June 19, 1940, after the amendment which I moved, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, was defeated by 202 against 2. That was a success. Is the government satisfied with its works? Will those who shared and are still sharing the most formidable responsibilities continue to vote with serene coolness the billions which are fatally leading us to the abyss?
Mr. Speaker, this deplorable picture of the actual situation will remain unchanged as long as our best energies remain paralyzed by a destructive policy. The lack of balance in our farm labour and our industrial labour is about

The Budget-Mr. Lacombe

to destroy the economic life of the country. From 1929 to 1939 we witnessed a great exodus of our rural population toward the cities. We saw hundreds of thousands of families on relief; thousands of labourers were out of work, and thousands of farmers were compelled to sell their farms because they could no longer make a living out of them. Confusion had set in everywhere. That was the post-war period, when the collapse was preceded by an artificial prosperity. What will the next postwar period bring us? Confusion, unemployment and anarchy, most likely.
How can we prevent these calamities? By taxing to the extreme limit those who take advantage of the war; by controlling and readjusting the salaries received by war workers; by exempting completely farmers from military training; and by granting the farmer and the labourer adequate representation in the cabinet. Briefly, by adopting social measures in accordance with the needs of the present and the requirements of to-morrow.
We shall not cure the great evils of this period with a multiplication of commissions of all kinds and with a bureaucracy which is not responsible to the people. We shall not improve this state of affairs by ignoring parliament. If we destroy responsible government we shall also destroy democracy. The united nations are fighting for democracy. Canada is fighting for its survival, and everything in this country seems to be conspiring to destroy it. Who could number the contradictions in the various attitudes taken by our statesmen? How many solemn pledges did they not violate? How many sacred commitments were not trampled upon? The country, which was already distrustful, is now wondering where the government is leading us.
The Minister of Finance attached great importance to the so-called extension granted to farmers in the paying of their income tax. We all know that the average farmer can barely make both ends meet, and how many still feel deeply the effects of the crisis, which lasted too long. When they were about to recover, the government deprived them of their best farmhands by calling their sons for military training. It also put a ceiling price on food. This ceiling price resulted in a discrepancy between ceiling prices of farm products and the purchasing price of foodstuffs, which I mentioned a while ago, the prices which must be paid for his clothing, that of his family, and those necessary objects he could not produce himself.
Furthermore, it is now impossible for them, and for quite a while they will not be able

to renew their farm implements, because the production of farm implements has been discontinued. In many districts they have been deprived of the privilege of developing their bushlands, because last fall the wartime prices and trade board set the price of cordwood so low that it was not worth while cutting any more. But the government got panicky and all of a sudden changed its mind. On March 4 it announced a subsidy of a dollar a cord on all cordwood. This was a useless measure, because it was taken too late. Last fall it practically killed all production of fuel wood, and now the government cannot redress the harm done to the trade and to industry, to the army and to the civilian population. This error cannot be rectified. How can the government now recover this cordwood which is definitely lost? Bushmen and farmers are now handicapped by snow, and in a few days there will be tremendous floods.
There is a time for everything, and I say to the Minister of Finance it is impossible to replace man-power and production by subsidies and orders in council. The government does not take into consideration the high cost of farm help. These powerful commissions which sometimes seem to ignore everything about agriculture have set ceiling prices on farm products and on cordwood, without giving due consideration to farm hands. As a consequence, in a few months we shall be facing a serious shortage of food and fuel. The government may boast of its love of the farmers and labourers, but those farmers and labourers will never swallow this heaviest and most insinuating budget the country has ever known.
You cannot tell the farmer, "I am granting you an extension to enable you to pay your income tax", because he will answer back "Give me back my best helpers, my sons whom you called up for military training; give me back my best farmhands, my most industrious and most experienced labour; give me the tools to produce, the tools for victory for which Mr. Churchill asked. My war work is to supply food to the army, to the industrial war workers and to the civilian population. You want me to pay income tax? Then take my farm; take this farm, which is only half cultivated because you did not allow me to do my share."
These are the complaints voiced by the agricultural classes in Canada. I do not invent them, and I do not betray them. The government has already heard those complaints, as voiced by the representatives of the people. Many requests have been sent in by agricultural associations; protests have come in from every district. Therefore the government can-

The Budget-Mr. Bence
not claim that it is not aware of these representations, all of which deal with matters of national importance.
(Translation): Before concluding my remarks, I cannot ignore the serious wrongs which constantly result from the thoughtless application of the mobilization act. I have so many times requested the government to transfer back to their respective fields of activity the farmers' sons and the war plants' workers now in training whose services are essential to the victory of our armed forces, that it would perhaps be idle to do it again Besides, mobilization means conscription. Is that not what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated himself during the debate on the repeal of section 3 of the mobilization act? That happened in July, 1942. There was a hectic atmosphere in this house, so much so that the Prime Minister reminded parliament that conscription had been in our statutes since June 21, 1940.
In conclusion, I shall quote an excerpt from "Relations" which strikingly resumes all the speeches delivered in parliament by those of my hon. fellow-members who are imbued with a truly Canadian spirit:
We know that Ulster, South Africa, India, and Australia, have not enacted conscription and as the Australians regret that they did not stay at home in order to defend their country, we hope that Canada will organize her own protection of the Maritime provinces and British Columbia, whose men are taken away. While appreciating devotion to the empire, we would rather protect our own interests. Gratitude for our hard-won survival, for theoretic or genuine rights does not imply for us the obligation to die for people who have neither killed nor deported us. In the words of Rene Johannet "an individual can or must, as the case may be, remain aloof. A group (a people) never has such a permission, which is the permission to commit suicide."
We do now disavow Sir John Macdonald's national policy; we have no desire to police the continents, or to redress world wrongs; we do not like to be handled like bundles by selfsatisfied colonials-from both parties-who know nothing of the Westminster Statute and who deal with us not in the tactful British manner, but with the harshness of "quality niggers" watching their brothers; we have no confidence in exclusive brain trusts whose stock is watered; we have read the militaristic epic of Sir Basil Zaharof, the Levantine who made millions out of the life blood of nations, and we fear that he may have emulators; we are the uncomplaining witnesses of the waste of military supplies- "Waste, the enemy at home", you say-and of the profits which are thereby made by Canadians too recently arrived in this country; we wish that the loan may be a success and that it may be better used; we bear insolence better than hypocrisy.

There are several matters with which I should like to deal in this debate, and it being impossible for me to complete the whole of my speech by eleven o'clock I wish to deal now with one particular phase which I believe is of the utmost importance to the farmers of the prairie provinces and to the citizens generally of that part of the country. It has to do with the production of flax for linseed oil. Flax is produced in this country for two purposes, one for the production of fibre and the other for the production of linseed oil. Flax for fibre is produced mainly in Ontario and Quebec; that for linseed oil is practically all grown in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. According to the information I have, which information I understand was produced to the agricultural conference held in Ottawa on December 9 last, in 1942 the seedings to flax in 1942 were:
Acres
Manitoba	 227,000
Alberta	 183,000
Saskatchewan	 1,056,000
The total Canadian flax acreage for last year was 1,492,000 acres.
As a result of the conquest by the Japanese of the sources of eastern vegetable oil supplies there was a great shortage of vegetable oils, and this continent found itself in a position where it had to accelerate its production of vegetable oils. It did so by various means. It endeavoured to increase the production of linseed oil as well as to produce a considerable quantity of oil from soya beans, sunflowers, and in the United States I understand that, in addition, they used peanuts. As a result of the requirement for greatly increased production, considerable stress was placed in the press and over the radio on this necessity. Therefore the farmers of the prairie provinces began to plan early last year for a tremendous increase in flax acreage. The return obtained from flax last year was very good; it was purposely good in order to increase the production as largely as possible. It seems to me and it seemed to the farmers on the prairies that the sensible and practical thing to do was to turn to production of flaxseed for oil purposes, something largely required for our war effort, and away from the production of wheat of which we have an overabundance and which constitutes perhaps the greatest agricultural problem in this country to-day.
I emphasize this point, that the farmers of western Canada during last summer and fall were planning for a large increase in flax acreage this year. They bought their seed,
The Budget-Mr. Bence

in many instances at fairly high prices, ranging I think from S3 to So, and by reason of the necessity for increased oil production from flax it was decided at an agricultural conference held in Ottawa on December 9, and I believe the following day or two, that the flax acreage for oil production should be increased in Canada by one million acres. Announcements were made to the press, and the farmers went on making plans for such production.
Then in the middle of January the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) rather suddenly made the statement that as a result of a conference held in Washington at which he was present it had been decided that no additional flax acreage should be put in during 1943. He stated that whereas the acreage in Canada in 1942 amounted to 1,492,000 acres and despite the fact that they had decided at this agricultural conference in December to increase the acreage to 2,500,000, at this conference held in Washington they found it was not feasible to cany out the increase that had been proposed, and he asked the farmers to go back to the original plan and produce from the same acreage as in 1942.
What I should like to know is why the Minister of Agriculture did not find out before January that it was not feasible to produce the additional acreage of flax which had been decided upon in Ottawa on December 9. After all, the United States had the whole key to the situation, and it seems to me they should have been consulted and that the Minister of Agriculture should have been fully aware of the situation which existed on December 9 when that conference was held in Ottawa. It is inconceivable to me that the authorities who had knowledge of the situation in Washington were not just as well aware at that time as they were a month later. The first announcement by the Minister of Agriculture that the plan arrived at on December 9 for the increased acreage would not be carried through was made at a meeting in the city of Saskatoon on January 14. I believe a similar announcement was made a day or two previously in Winnipeg, though I have not the press reference in that connection. Then to further confuse the situation, on January 17 there was a press release from the publicity and extension service of the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa, which was referred to in an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune under date of February 6, as follows:
The United States department of agriculture, according to the latest survey, estimates that that country faces a shortage of close to a billion pounds of fats and oils for food and

industrial purposes in 1943. To help overcome this shortage the government of Canada is asking for increased production of oil-producing plants such as flax, soybeans, sunflowers, etc. The objective for flaxseed is an acreage increase of 68 per cent.
This was just three days after the minister had made the statement that there was to be no increase in acreage for 1943. Then on January 29 the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), speaking in this house on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture, in effect stated that there was no assurance that flaxseed from any additional acreage could be disposed of in 1943. Then to confuse the situation even more, on March 1 there appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix a dispatch from Ottawa under the heading "Flaxseed campaign expected" as follows:
Definite announcement is expected in a few days that Canada will launch a flaxseed campaign this year to increase sown acreage by
1.000.	000 acres. In 1942 flax acreage was
1.500.000	acres, and the 1943 objective is ex-jiected to be not less than 2,500,000 acres.
The flaxseed situation is rapidly clarifying, it is learned, and the original production objective of the Department of Agriculture is expected to be retained. In December the department called for an increase of 68 per cent in flax acreage, but in January plans were revised though the final 1943 objective was left open.
Last Tuesday Doctor Phyllis Turner, Canadian administrator of oils and fats, stated in a Toronto speech that Canada's minimum requirements of flaxseed would be 20,000,000 bushels. Confirming this to-day, she said this meant
2.500.000	acres would be required. Disposal of
20.000.	000 bushels of Canadian flax grown in 1943 could be made, said Mrs. Turner, to fill Canadian, American and British requirements.
Then on March 3 in the same newspaper there appeared a press dispatch dealing with a meeting of the national barley and linseed flax committee at Winnipeg, in which reference is made to a statement by Mr. L. H. Lehberg, as follows:
L. H. Lehberg, technical adviser to the federal oils and fats administration, told the committee's annual meeting that supplies of vegetable oils received from the United States had been below expectations and that U.S. crushers were in the market for Canadian flax in addition to overseas demand.
In addition to domestic supplies, there were indications that upwards of 10,000,000 bushels of flax will be wanted by the United States and a like amount wanted for export overseas it was stated.
Yesterday I managed to ask the Minister of Agriculture if he would make a statement in this connection, since I believed it imperative that the whole matter should be cleared up as soon as possible in order that the farmers of the prairie provinces might know their position, but the only response I could

Questions
obtain was in effect that a statement would be made before seeding time. I do not believe the farmers should be treated in what I might describe as this rather cavalier fashion. If administrators and officials of various departments, who are supposed to have knowledge of this matter, are making statements to the press that this increase in acreage is to be brought about, surely the farmers should be given the definite information by the minister himself as soon as possible. I think Mr. George W. Robertson, secretary of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, put the matter very clearly in a radio address on January 15, during which he referred to the necessity for early knowledge on the part of the farmer in order that he might make his plans for the coming year. Mr. Robertson said:
There is amongst western farmers a feeling of confusion as to just where they fit into the general picture. This is illustrated by the flax situation. With limited manpower, limited ability to secure the implements of production, if we are to obtain maximum farm output there must be a very great deal of careful preparation carried on by the producers themselves. Plans cannot be adjusted at a moment's notice and farmers have a right to know what this country expects of them.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I should like to know, and I am sure the farmers would like to know, just what took place at that Washington conference early in January and why it was decided at that time not to increase production. Was it on account of lack of crushers? It may have been. How has the picture changed between January 1 and the present time?
